title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

summary.text: This ground investigation aims to quantify how external thermal and convective perturbations affect established droplet cool flames, using a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity.

geometry.text: Large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

pressure.text: Pressure and ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases) are varied in parameter sweeps.

flow.text: Convection alone is applied to mimic droplet drift.

measurements.text: Predictive observables extracted: ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters.

claims.text: This ground investigation aims to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulate the dynamics and fate of established droplet cool flames.
External thermo-convective perturbations were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction.
The metadata states the work has potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame and extinction behavior in microgravity (stated as a research impact, not as a result).

limitations.text: The approach describes a computational model and its planned observables; the metadata states no numerical result.
Only PSI metadata was examined; no document text was processed, so statements are limited to what the metadata fields say.

modeling_resources.description: Candidate data for modeling: extinction diameter and burning-history files for droplet cool flames from the simulation analyses. No model validation is claimed.

evidence.excerpt: to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity

External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction
